message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold a maximum of **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a furnished unit).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a safe, sanitary, and livable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• Repairs must be made within a reasonable time after you notify the landlord. | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) and keep a copy.
• If repairs are not made, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable (usually not more than 5% of the rent). | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Report any harassment or unlawful entry. | | **Landlord Entry** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries and request a written notice if you suspect unlawful entry. | | **Privacy** | • Landlords cannot enter your unit without notice, except in emergencies. | • If you suspect unlawful entry, document the incident and consider filing a complaint. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party can terminate a lease with proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month).
• Landlords must provide a written notice of termination. | • Keep copies of all notices and confirm receipt. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, provided you follow the proper procedure. | • Document the defect, notify the landlord, keep receipts, and provide a written notice of your intent to repair and deduct. | | **Rent Increase** | • For month‑to‑month leases, landlords must give at least **30 days’ notice** before increasing rent. | • Review the lease for any rent‑increase clauses and verify that the notice period is met. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas eviction procedure: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for nonpayment), file a lawsuit, and obtain a court order. | • Respond to notices promptly, attend court hearings, and keep records of all communications. | | **Legal Remedies** | • You can sue for unpaid rent, damages, or breach of contract.
• Small claims court can handle disputes up to $20,000. | • File a claim in the appropriate county court and keep all documentation. | | **Reporting Problems** | • File complaints with TDHCA for habitability issues.
• File complaints with TCHR for discrimination.
• File complaints with local housing authorities for code violations. | • Use online portals or call the relevant agency. | #### Quick Tips 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – It’s the primary source of your rights and responsibilities. 2. **Keep Written Records** – Emails, texts, and written notices are your best evidence. 3. **Know the Notice Periods** – Texas law requires specific notice periods for rent increases, entry, and termination. 4. **Seek Legal Aid if Needed** – Many nonprofits offer free or low‑cost legal assistance to tenants. 5. **Use Official Channels** – File complaints through TDHCA, TCHR, or local housing authorities for official support. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is general in nature and not legal advice. For specific legal questions, consult a licensed attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.
